newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Iraq sees unchanged US stance on oil in 96.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Iraq sees unchanged US stance on oil in 96.

text.p: Iraq's chief negotiator with the United Nations said on Thursday that he did not expect any change in the U.S. position on the oil-for-food deal until January 1997 at the earliest.
In an interview with Reuters, Ambassador Abdul Amir al-Anbari put the full blame on Washington for the delay in implementing the stalled humanitarian accord signed last May.
Citing recent U.N. estimates that thousands of Iraqi children are dying each month for lack of food and medicine, he called it a "slow, steady if not deliberate genocide against the Iraqi people".
Al-Anbari was in Geneva to lead an Iraqi delegation to a two-day seminar on the impact of international sanctions, sponsored by the Swiss-based Crans-Montana forum.

Under the limited agreement with the United Nations, Iraq would be allowed to export $2 billion of oil over renewable six-month periods so as to buy sorely-needed food and medicine to ease the effects of sanctions on ordinary civilians.

Al-Anbari dismissed as a "cover-up" allegations by U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright that President Saddam Hussein was deliberately holding up the deal by making what she called "outrageous demands" on U.N. staff assigned to monitor it.
"Iraq had presented a pricing formula and is ready to go ahead with oil sale once the pricing formula is approved by the United States," he told Reuters.

Asked when he expected the deal to be implemented, he replied: "Actually, it is up to the United States because only the United States has refused to approve the pricing formula presented by Iraq to the Sanctions Committee.
"They don't even say why they don't approve it."
Al-Anbari, asked whether he expected any breakthrough in implementing the pact before an OPEC ministerial meeting on November 27, replied: "I hope so, but frankly I doubt it.

"I believe the U.S. is holding their position until January 1997. They have not indicated this, but this is how I read their position from past experience," added al-Anbari, who led Iraq's team during the New York negotiations between February and May.

Al-Anbari said the United States was alone in rejecting the pricing formula proposed by Baghdad which would be used in oil sales contracts. But Albright last week dismissed the oil-pricing controversy as a "phony issue" raised by Iraq.

Most diplomats prefer to endorse the formula in advance so their oil experts can approve sales contracts quickly once the deal goes through. In August, when the last pricing formula was presented, only the United States delayed approval.
The committee last week received a new pricing plan, but Albright said at the time the issue was academic while Iraq was issuing unacceptable demands.
The U.N. Security Council's sanctions committee has to unanimously approve any pricing formula that changes each month based on trading values of oil from a number of regions.

Al-Anbari, asked whether he expected any change in the U.S. policy with President Clinton's re-election, said: "I believe he will address the matter on merit and take into consideration the legality as well as humanitarian aspects of the sanctions."

"The sanctions on Iraq are the most inhumane sanctions because they deprive Iraq of any penny in order to buy food and medicine. It is simply a slow, steady if not deliberate genocide against the Iraqi people," he added.

U.N. aid agencies last week expressed alarm at the lack of food, medicine and clean water in Iraq, estimating that 4,500 children under age five were dying monthly in part because of stringent trade sanctions.
"Even if we start implementing the memo of understanding, food and medicine would not be arriving in Iraq until say two or three or four months later," al-Anbari said.

"So the suffering would continue for a long time, plus the quantities to be imported are only nominal compared to the real requirements of 20 million people who have been under sanctions for six years," he said.
At its regular 60-day review, the U.N. Security Council last Friday renewed blanket economic sanctions imposed on Iraq since its invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.
Albright accused Iraq of deliberately blocking the deal by making outrageous demands on U.N. staff assigned to monitor it.

These included replacing all local staff members the United Naitons had hired, cutting its 150-person monitoring staff nearly in half, curtailing monitors' freedom of movement and making Baghdad the beneficiary of a U.N. escrow account set up to receive the oil revenues.
Albright also denied allegations that the Clinton administration was delaying the deal.
